steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Intro
- Internet era: access to information never so convenient; huge numbers of users online for entertainment or business
- organizations offer products/services online to grow customer base
- customers usually sign up and must agree to term-and-conditions (T&C) / policies
- privacy policy: lets organization legally collect, process, store, distribute personal information; how data handled, compliance with data protection laws
- customers grant access to sensitive data (name, contact information, location) without reading/understanding the policy
- some companies collect data with distributional rights, sell user data to third parties with inadvertent consent
- reasons: busy schedules; lengthy, technical/legal language

## Motivation and Problem Definition
- businesses: protection from legal issues on data privacy/usage
- individuals: transparency on how personal info managed/protected -> informed decisions before registering
- very few users read these documents
- summarization = straightforward remedy, but every aspect of data usage/management must be in summary
- hard: data items (name, age, contact details) defined at start, their management reported only at end or in different paragraph/context
- controlled abstractive summarization can improve accessibility, transparency
- EROS: Entity-dRiven cOntrolled policy document Summarization
- stage 1: extract entities/data items and rationales with BERT and XLNet-based entity-extraction module
- stage 2: BART-based summarization module forced to include entities + rationales via PPO
- PD-Sum: 1900 policy documents, manual abstractive summaries + privacy-related entities and rationales
- mark all entities; identify what, why, how collected; schema (Figure; Section 3)
- schema: data collected, source of data, medium of collection, consumer (target), reason for collection
- annotated example in Figure
- then write summary mandating entities + rationales + other relevant info
- results: state-of-the-art on PD-Sum vs several baselines; qualitative and error analyses

## Contribution
- EROS (BART-based) to address public concerns over data privacy and security
- EEPD entity extraction model
- personalized loss + RL with PPO for relevance and length
- PD-Sum dataset
- performance benchmarks vs baselines
- qualitative and error analyses

## Reproducibility
- https://github.com/joykirat18/EROS

- summary written mandating entities + rationales

- EROS (BART-based) for public data privacy/security concerns

- personalized loss + PPO reinforcement learning (relevance, length)
- PD-Sum dataset
- benchmarks vs baselines
- qualitative + error analyses

- code + data: https://github.com/joykirat18/EROS

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the Internet era today, it has never been so convenient to access information. Every day a huge number of users explore the Internet for entertainment or for business. Many organizations see this as a great opportunity to grow their customer base, so they offer their products or services in a convenient online setting. In most cases customers have to sign up to get the services on offer, and when they do this they have to agree to the term-and-conditions (T&C) or policies of the service providers.

A privacy policy is a crucial part of any organization, since it allows the organization to legally collect, process, store, and/or distribute personal information. It describes how the organization will handle personal data and how it will comply with the data protection laws and regulations that apply. What customers often don't know is that on many occasions they are, advertently or inadvertently, giving the service providers full access to their sensitive and private data (e.g., name, contact information, location, etc.) without reading or understanding the privacy policy document. Also, some companies collect data with distributional rights too and make a lot of money by selling user's data to third parties without the users realizing it, but with their inadvertent consent. The main reason users ignore this is their busy and packed schedule, and also the lengthy and technical/legal language, which is usually hard for a common user to understand.

## Motivation and Problem Definition:

Privacy policies are essential both for businesses and for individuals. For businesses, a privacy policy can protect them from legal issues about data privacy and usage. For individuals, it gives transparency about how their personal information will be managed and protected by the organizations, so they can make informed decisions before registering for the service. But even though they are important, very few users read these long and non-trivial documents, and they fall prey to their inadvertent consent.

Summarizing these documents is a straightforward remedy for the long document, but it has to make sure that every aspect of data usage/management is also in the summary, otherwise it is not useful. Because the policy document is complicated, it is non-trivial to get every critical privacy-related information into a summary. For example, some policy documents define different data items (like name, age, contact details, etc.) at the beginning of the document but don't report how the data items are managed until the end of the document or in a different paragraph or context, which makes it hard for any summarization system to deal with these cases. In these cases controlled abstractive summarization techniques can potentially improve accessibility and transparency by generating concise and coherent summaries of policy documents. Because the problem is severe, in this paper we propose an Entity-dRiven cOntrolled policy document Summarization system, or EROS. EROS works in two stages: 1) it extracts different entities or data items and their rationales with a BERT and XLNet-based entity-extraction module; and 2) using the extracted entities, it forces a BART-based summarization module to include these entities and their rationales through a proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework.

We developed a dataset called PD-Sum, of 1900 policy documents, and we manually annotated them with abstractive summaries and with privacy-related entities and their rationales. First we mark all the entities in the document and we also identify what, why, and how they are being collected. To do this we proposed and followed a schema for identifying critical privacy-related information in a policy document, as shown in Figure (see Section 3 for details). It includes the data being collected, who the source of the data is, through which medium the data will be collected, who will consume (target) the data, and what the reason for collecting the data is. An example with annotated entities is shown in Figure. In the next step we write a summary of the document that has to contain the entities and their rationales together with other relevant information.

Our experiments show that EROS gets state-of-the-art performance on the proposed PD-Sum dataset compared to several baseline systems. We also do qualitative and error analyses to check how well EROS ensures the different aspects of privacy-related information in the generated summaries.

## Contribution:

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

- • We propose a BART-based entity-driven controlled policy document summarization (EROS) to address the concerns of the general public about data privacy and security issues.

- • We developed an entity extraction model, Entity Extraction from Policy Documents (EEPD), to identify relevant privacy-related information in a policy document.

- • We introduce a personalized loss function and a reinforcement learning framework with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to manage how relevant and how long the generated summaries are.

- • We introduce a new dataset (PD-Sum) of privacy policy documents with their summaries and privacy-bounded entities and rationales.

- • We also set performance benchmarks for the proposed approach against several baselines.

- • Finally, we do qualitative and error analyses to check the quality of the summaries.

## Reproducibility:

The code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/joykirat18/EROS.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In today's Internet era, access to information has never been so convenient. Every day, an overwhelming number of users explore the Internet for entertainment or business purposes. Seeing an excellent opportunity to increase their customer base, many organizations offer their products or services in a convenient online setting. In most cases, customers are required to sign up to acquire the services on offer, and in doing so they have to agree to the term-and-conditions (T&C) or policies of the service providers.

A privacy policy is a crucial component of any organization that allows it to legally collect, process, store, and/or distribute personal information. It outlines how an organization will handle personal data and how it will comply with applicable data protection laws and regulations. Little do they know that, on many occasions, customers are, advertently or inadvertently, granting the service providers full access to their sensitive and private data (e.g., name, contact information, location, etc.) without reading or understanding the privacy policy document. Moreover, some companies also collect data with distributional rights and make a fortune by selling users' data to third parties without their realization but with their inadvertent consent. The primary reason for such ignorance on the user's part is their busy and packed schedule, as well as the lengthy and technical/legal language, which is usually difficult for a common user to comprehend.

## Motivation and Problem Definition:

Privacy policies are essential for both businesses and individuals. For businesses, a privacy policy can protect them from legal issues related to data privacy and usage. For individuals, it provides transparency about how their personal information will be managed and protected by organizations, thus enabling them to make informed decisions before registering for the service. Despite this importance, very few users read these lengthy and non-trivial documents, and they fall prey to their inadvertent consent.

Summarizing these documents is a straightforward remedy for their length, but the summary must include every aspect of data usage/management to be useful. Given the complicated nature of policy documents, however, it is non-trivial to capture every critical piece of privacy-related information in a summary. For instance, some policy documents define different data items (viz. name, age, contact details, etc.) at the beginning of the document but do not report how these items are managed until the end of the document, or in a different paragraph or context, making it challenging for any summarization system to handle such cases. In such cases, controlled abstractive summarization techniques [1,2,3] can potentially enhance accessibility and transparency by generating concise and coherent summaries of policy documents. Acknowledging the severity of the problem, in this paper we propose an Entity-dRiven cOntrolled policy document Summarization system, aka EROS. EROS operates in two stages: 1) it extracts various entities or data items and their rationales through a BERT and XLNet-based entity-extraction module; and 2) leveraging the extracted entities, it mandates a BART-based summarization module to include these entities and their rationales through a proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework.

We developed a dataset, namely PD-Sum, of 1900 policy documents and manually annotated them with abstractive summaries along with privacy-related entities and their rationales. First, we mark all entities present in the document and identify what, why, and how they are being collected. To this end, we proposed and followed a schema for identifying critical privacy-related information in a policy document, as depicted in Figure (c.f. Section 3 for details). It covers the data being collected, the source of the data, the medium through which data will be collected, who will consume (target) the data, and the reason for data collection. An example with annotated entities is shown in Figure. In the next step, we write a summary of the document mandating the presence of the entities and their rationales along with other relevant information.

Our experimental results show that EROS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the proposed PD-Sum dataset against several baseline systems. We also perform qualitative and error analyses to assess the capability of EROS in ensuring the various aspects of privacy-related information in the generated summaries.

## Contribution:

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

- • We propose a BART-based entity-driven controlled policy document summarization (EROS) to mitigate the general public's concerns over data privacy and security issues.

- • To identify relevant privacy-related information in a policy document, we developed an entity extraction model, Entity Extraction from Policy Documents (EEPD).

- • We introduce a personalized loss function and a reinforcement learning framework using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to manage the relevance and length of the generated summaries.

- • We introduce a new dataset (PD-Sum) of privacy policy documents with their summaries and privacy-bounded entities and rationales.

- • We also establish performance benchmarks for the proposed approach against several baselines.

- • Finally, we perform qualitative and error analyses to assess the quality of the summaries.

## Reproducibility:

Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/joykirat18/EROS.

[2] Liu and Chen (2021) Zhengyuan Liu and Nancy F. Chen. 2021. Controllable neural dialogue summarization with personal named entity planning . In Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing .
